title: Martina Navratilova on Chris Evert, their rivalry and beating cancer

segments.transcript: Martina Navratilova was a high-profile force on the tennis court in the 1970s and 80s,
With 59 grand slam titles, including 18 in singles, 31 in doubles, and 10 in mixed doubles.
She's remained a big presence in the tennis world, commentating and mentoring, and also using her platform to weigh in on issues off the court as well.
I caught up with her recently at the U.S.
Open in New York for our ongoing culture of sport coverage, part of our Canvas series.
In the tennis world, this is hallowed ground.
Flushing Meadows, New York, the site of Martina Navratilova's very last match,
A mixed doubles win at the 2006 U.S. Open.
Oh, center court is here at 10 o'clock at night.
I mean, I usually get really nervous before matches, but I was excited and least nervous that I've been and played really well.
These days, she's courtside behind a microphone, watching today's tennis stars own the spotlight.
But a recent critically acclaimed Netflix documentary, Chris and Martina, turned the spotlight back on her,
Capturing the intense rivalry between Martina and Chris Ever, whose win-loss record in singles is the best of any pro player,
Male or female, in history.
That was the first real rivalry that sparked that type of interest.
It's a film about fierce competitors who also formed a deep and abiding friendship.
How did those two coexist over that time? You're only as good as your opponent. You cannot hit great shots.
You cannot be pushed to great heights unless you have the opponent that makes you have to do that. So, we made each other better.
And I think we understood that, even though we didn't kind of appreciate it maybe that much during the...
Oh, my God, I got to play Chris again, you know, another two and a half on our match.
And it was always so physical playing her because she doesn't miss.
So the contrast in styles was really obvious.
We appreciated each other always and respected each other.
Navratilova was just 18 when she made the tough choice to defect from then-communist Czechoslovakia.
She was playing under temporary U.S. Residency.
Alone in the U.S., she set her sights on beating then-number-one Chris Ever. Yes.
Chris was a lot more switched on to the emotional and mental state of the game.
I mean, I controlled my emotions at the end, but it took me a while. And also, I was alone. I didn't have a coach.
I didn't have anybody to tell me, hey, listen, you're just beating yourself.
There was also this narrative of sort of the American girly girl versus the tough communist player.
The media really fueled that. I mean, did you feel that?
Were they trying to get you to say things about each other?
Oh, they were writing one kind of story, and then once I lived here, it was like, oh, look at all the jewelry she's wearing.
And I went from a communist to a capitalist with nothing in between, and I'm neither.
The press was definitely feeding off of the contrast.
And it was hard, because there literally was one guy that wrote good versus evil.
Over 80 matches against each other, their bond grew and deepened as their careers came to a close.
So, once you retired, you know, all the walls came down.
And then, once I retired, then we could really reminisce and be close. But we always trusted each other.
There was always a trust that I had with Chris that never went away, that I felt, if the push comes to shove,
She's one of the people I can call, and she would be there for me.
They faced their toughest battles yet together, early stage breast cancer and stage one throat cancer for Navratilova,
And ovarian cancer for Evert, a third round she announced in June. I'm all free. You're good. You're in the clear.
Everything I just have to do, breast cancer screenings every six months, rather than once a year. I'm on the lucky spectrum.
Chris had a more difficult cancer, but she's tough, and she's going to be OK.
How often do you two talk to each other?
We stay in touch through text all the time, and we speak maybe once a week, once every two weeks.
So I'll see her after the open and make some more pesto for her because she likes my pesto That's what you make for his pesto Martina tennis is such a lonely sport, right?

You're out there alone you win and you lose and you're alone and when you're going through your cancer battles it was almost as if only the two of you could understand what each other was going through you get used to that solitude
And problem-solving on the court and You know staying staying positive when things don't go right otherwise you would not be winning these matches at the end of the day and so
This is just another match where it's not that much in your control but the the attitude and the getting the solution our mindset was all is is still there this is more life and death situation but
Still you kind of get on with it and stay very very positive and that makes a big difference at the end.
Navratilova herself made a difference for millions as a publicly gay sports star outed against her will in 1981.
There was a New York Times piece that said,
Homosexuality is the most sensitive issue in the sports marketplace, more delicate than drugs, more controversial than violence.
I mean, that was the environment at the time.
A hundred percent, if a guy got caught shooting somebody, it was less of a problem than being gay.
Homosexuality was just a plague.
It was leprosy and cancer and all of that bass stuff put together.
Those people were not to be touched in any way or acknowledged.
So, but I mean, I was outed, but I wanted to stay in the closet for the tour, not for myself. I didn't care.
And on the public space, it was a big no-no.
And it hurt me financially.
I didn't get any endorsements because of that, but I could still play tennis, and that was the biggest thing for me, you know.
So I always encourage people to come out if they can.
If they can still do their job and not get fired for it, please come out if you possibly can.
But on the question of transgender athletes competing in women's sports, Nevratilova has been firm in her opposition and faced heavy criticism for it.
You wrote an op-ed in 2019.
You said that trans women competing in female categories was the same as cheating, basically.
You said, I'm happy to address a transgender woman in whatever form she prefers.
I would not be happy to compete against her. It would not be fair.
That was a few years ago, so do you still feel the same today?
If they undergo all this drug stuff, taking hormones for a longer period of time,
Could we make it a fair fight?
Could they be included in a fair way in women's sport?
And then we talk, oh, maybe we handicap this, handicap that, but on a team sport it cannot work.
Individual, you can't, but how do you measure that?
And at the end of the day we realize there is no way to include males,
However they identify in female sports, because the bodies are just two different things, and it cannot ever be a fair fight.
I know you've spent so much of your career and your platform advocating for LGBTQ rights.
You've been an ally for so many people, and as you know, one of those groups came out cut ties with you after these comments.
They said that your words are transphobic and they worried it would help fuel discrimination and violence against transgender people. How do you feel about that?
So women's sex based spaces need to stay for women,
But everywhere else, trans, however they identify, cannot be fired for doing their job.
If they're doing their job, you cannot be firing people because they're trans or identify as non-binary or whatever.
So all the rights to every job they have, but female sex based spaces,
Which includes sports, that's a step too far because then you are excluding women.
So, you cannot be encroaching on our spaces at the expense of making them comfortable.
This summer, tennis became the first major women's sports league to require genetic testing.
One advocacy group said that testing, quote, invades all women's privacy, forcing them to give up their personal medical and genetic information.
Navratilova is undeterred by the backlash.
The ferocious competitor in her made it to number one, beat cancer, and is now watching a new generation claim its place in history.
Does the part of you still wish you were out there?
Like, do you have to keep yourself from running out on the court? If I could still play, I would.
At the same time, I'm so happy I don't have that stress.
So I'm good where I am, but I love to be a part of this sport that gave me my life.
And I'm happy to give something back.
